segments.text: > Part of the [Implementation Status](README.md) index. The piece that unlocks this project's microservice direction. Full design: [TDD-00004](../tdd/TDD-00004.md).

The Node `http` module exposes only the **real Node.js API** — `http.createServer`/`get`/`request`/`Agent`. The bespoke `http.listen(handler ⇒ response)` model (the rest of this page) is this project's own re-imagining, reachable **only** under the explicitly-non-Node `klain:http` specifier now ([TDD-00131](../tdd/TDD-00131.md)/[ADR-00635](../adr/ADR-00635.md)) — it is no longer exposed on `http` (Node has `listen`/`close`/`closeAllConnections` as `Server` methods, not `http.*` functions). Importing them from `http` is a clean rejection pointing at `klain:http`.

caveats: Windows keeps the earlier code-generated server (the TCP handles are POSIX sockets)
notes: Node's `_http_common`/`_http_incoming`/`_http_outgoing`/`_http_server` ported to TypeScript (`lib/node/internal_http.ts`) over `net` and a native HTTP/1 parser with llhttp's strict rules and `HPE_*` codes: `req` is an `IncomingMessage` (a Readable — `'data'`/`'end'`, `pipe`, `for await`, `headers`/`rawHeaders`/`trailers`), `res` a `ServerResponse` (`writeHead`/`setHeader`/`appendHeader`/`getHeader(s)`/`write`/`end`/`flushHeaders`/`writeContinue`, chunked or `Content-Length`, back-pressure and `'drain'`), keep-alive and pipelining, `Date`, `requireHostHeader`'s 400 ([ADR-01170](../adr/ADR-01170.md))
An `async` handler is an ordinary callback: the server keeps serving while it awaits

caveats: The `IncomingMessage`/`ServerResponse` options (custom classes) are not accepted
`res.setHeaders` takes a `Map` only — a `Headers` argument is a union code generation cannot tell apart ([BACKLOG](../BACKLOG.md))
notes: `listen` as `net.Server.listen` (port, host, backlog, options object, path; `'listening'` and `'error'` on the next tick, as Node emits them); events `'request'`, `'connection'`, `'upgrade'`, `'connect'`, `'checkContinue'`, `'checkExpectation'`, `'clientError'` (Node's 400/408/431 without a listener), `'dropRequest'`, `'close'`; `close`/`closeAllConnections`/`closeIdleConnections`/`setTimeout`

Options `requestTimeout`/`headersTimeout` (swept every `connectionsCheckingInterval` by an unref'd timer, as Node does), `keepAliveTimeout` (+ `keepAliveTimeoutBuffer`), `maxHeaderSize`, `maxRequestsPerSocket`, `joinDuplicateHeaders`, `requireHostHeader`, `noDelay`, `keepAlive`, `highWaterMark`, `rejectNonStandardBodyWrites` ([ADR-01170](../adr/ADR-01170.md))
One fiber per accepted connection (`ucontext.h`), so a slow connection never blocks the others
Runs on the shared `select()` event loop with timers, fetch, and the other socket APIs

`fork()`s `N-1` workers sharing the listening socket — parallelism across cores on top of each process's own fiber concurrency. On Windows (no `fork()`) the workers are re-spawned processes and the primary deals connections out round-robin, itself included ([ADR-01027](../adr/ADR-01027.md))
`cluster.isPrimary`/`cluster.worker` (undefined in the original process, the Worker with ids 1..N-1 in each fork) branch on the current process
Works under both memory modes
A worker exits (status 0) once its primary is gone, as Node's cluster worker does when its channel disconnects — it does not keep the port open ([ADR-01042](../adr/ADR-01042.md))

May be combined with Node `http.createServer` servers in one program — declared after them, the cluster joins the shared reactor as an additional listener and the fork runs once every listener is bound, so each worker serves every port; the combined program cannot also use Worker *threads* (`fork()` + threads is unsafe) ([ADR-00989](../adr/ADR-00989.md))
Any method token (`GET`/`POST`/`PUT`/`DELETE`/...), not GET-only
`req.path` excludes the query string (that's `req.query`)
Lowercased keys (case-insensitive lookup, matching real HTTP semantics) — [ADR-00072](../adr/ADR-00072.md)
Split from `req.path` and parsed (`a=b&c=d`), both keys and values percent-decoded via the same `decodeURIComponent` primitive this compiler already had — [ADR-00072](../adr/ADR-00072.md)
`Content-Length`-aware, accumulated across reads, capped at 10MiB — [ADR-00072](../adr/ADR-00072.md)

Binary-safe: the buffer, the `string` value, and every string operation carry/read a length header, so an embedded null byte survives — an `"ab\0cd"` body reports length 5 and echoes 5 bytes ([TDD-00120](../tdd/TDD-00120.md)/[ADR-00364](../adr/ADR-00364.md))

Wraps the same already-buffered, `Content-Length`-accurate bytes into an `ArrayBuffer` (no copy) — an explicit `ArrayBuffer` view for callers that want one; `req.body: string` is itself binary-safe now ([TDD-00120](../tdd/TDD-00120.md))
Fully user-controlled, including `Content-Type` if set — omitting the field behaves byte-identically to before this existed — [ADR-00072](../adr/ADR-00072.md)

Wins outright over `body`'s own content whenever present and non-null — the response writer (`__kml_http_send_response`) writes the body via an explicit-length `write()` (not a NUL-terminated `sprintf %s`), so a binary payload with embedded null bytes reaches the socket whole

The plain string `body` field is itself binary-safe now — it too writes via the header length, so `bodyBytes` is an explicit-`ArrayBuffer` convenience rather than the only NUL-safe path ([TDD-00120](../tdd/TDD-00120.md)/[ADR-00364](../adr/ADR-00364.md))

rows.feature: Streaming response body (`body: ReadableStream<string \| Uint8Array>` field)
notes: A handler whose returned object's `body` field is statically a `ReadableStream` produces a `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` response, written chunk-at-a-time by a promise-reaction-driven writer — the handler returns immediately and a slow producer holds only its own connection open; `http.close()` still waits for in-flight streams
A stream error mid-response closes the connection without the chunked terminator (nothing else is signallable mid-stream)
See [ADR-00300](../adr/ADR-00300.md)

rows.feature: Streaming request body (`req.stream(): ReadableStream<Uint8Array>`, or `req` as a Node `Readable`)
notes: The server `req` is a Node `Readable` over its own body ([TDD-00195](../tdd/TDD-00195.md) Stage 1, [ADR-00824](../adr/ADR-00824.md)): `for await (const chunk of req)`, `req.on('data'|'end')`, and `req.pipe(dest)` all consume the same underlying stream (`Uint8Array` chunks), cached on first use so they don't double-consume
`req.body`/`req.bodyBytes()` after consuming `req.stream()` throw a catchable `TypeError` (WHATWG "body already disturbed", [ADR-00362](../adr/ADR-00362.md))

A handler may mix response `body` shapes across branches by declaring a union `body: string \| ReadableStream<Uint8Array>` — the writer branches on the runtime tag ([TDD-00119](../tdd/TDD-00119.md)/[ADR-00363](../adr/ADR-00363.md))

Using `req.stream()` anywhere switches the program to headers-complete dispatch: the handler runs once headers are parsed and the body flows as `Uint8Array` chunks read off the socket (fiber-yield on EAGAIN, event-loop pump for non-fiber consumers); the 10MiB request cap then applies to the header block only
`req.body`/`req.bodyBytes()` stay correct — they drain the remaining body into the pre-allocated buffer in place
`req.stream()` piped into a streaming response body echoes without ever buffering the payload

The handler runs from ordinary control flow at the top of a loop iteration (never real signal context) and may clean up and `process.exit()` — [TDD-00019](../tdd/TDD-00019.md)/[ADR-00079](../adr/ADR-00079.md), [PROCESS-CLI.md](PROCESS-CLI.md)

rows.feature: `http.close()` (formal listener teardown, distinct from the graceful-shutdown row above)
notes: A bare global function (like `http.listen` itself), reachable only from inside a running request handler, `setTimeout`/`setInterval` callback, or `process.on(...)` handler — the only places code ever runs "alongside" the event loop

Graceful by design: stops accepting immediately and lets already-open connections finish before `http.listen()`'s own call returns control to the rest of the program (matching Node's default `server.close()`) — `http.closeAllConnections()` (next row) is the forceful counterpart

In a `{ workers: N }` cluster, one worker's `.close()` shuts down every worker — it sets a shared flag page (`mmap`'d under `fork()`, a named section on Windows) each worker's event loop polls, so the whole cluster drains and exits with no external signal ([TDD-00117](../tdd/TDD-00117.md)/[ADR-00359](../adr/ADR-00359.md))

The forceful counterpart to `http.close()` (Node's `server.closeAllConnections()`): `shutdown(2)`s every in-flight connection so each fiber unwinds through its own EOF finish path — no suspended-fiber teardown from outside
Shuts down the calling handler's own connection too (Node parity), so send the response before calling it if the response must be delivered
In a `{ workers: N }` cluster, one worker's call force-closes every worker's connections via the same shared `mmap` flag `http.close()` uses (word[1])
